propositions.text: SOCAN initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board to set royalty rates for 2014–2026 for online audiovisual and user-generated content services.
propositions.quote: The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board seeking an order of the Board establishing the royalty rates (i.e., setting tariffs) SOCAN will collect for 2014–2026 from users of musical works in online audiovisual services and user-generated content services.

propositions.text: The Copyright Board has authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act.
propositions.quote: The Copyright Board has the authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN started a proceeding before the Copyright Board to set online royalty rates, which the Board is authorized to do under the Copyright Act.

propositions.text: The Board divided the proceeding into two phases and identified four preliminary issues for Phase I.
propositions.quote: the Board decided to divide the proceeding into two phases and identified “four preliminary issues” to be considered in Phase I

propositions.text: The four preliminary issues include the application of CBC v SODRAC, statutory exceptions, interpretation of s. 66.501(a), and rights triggered by offline viewing copies.
propositions.quote: 1. Does the Supreme Court’s decision in CBC v SODRAC, 2015 SCC 57, apply to tariff proceedings before the Board? If so, how? 2. Is it possible for the statutory exceptions (listed in the Order) [ss. 29.21, 29.24, 30.7, 30.71 and 31.1 of the Copyright Act] to apply to a class of services covered by the Proposed Tariffs? 3. What is the interpretation of paragraph 66.501(a) of the [the Act]? 4. When offline viewing copies are offered, created, and used, which rights are triggered?

propositions.text: These issues are summarized in Notice CB-CDA 2024-061 and Ruling CB-CDA 2025-109.
propositions.quote: Notice CB-CDA 2024-061, dated July 24, 2024 (Phase I Notice), as summarized in Ruling CB-CDA 2025-109, dated November 21, 2025.

paragraphs.summary: The Board split the proceeding into two phases, listing four preliminary issues for Phase I, as summarized in official notices and rulings.

propositions.text: The Board included two safeguards in the Phase I Notice in response to parties' concerns.
propositions.quote: the Board’s Phase I Notice included what it described as two safeguards

propositions.text: The second safeguard allows parties to ask the Board to reconsider Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence significantly throws them into doubt.
propositions.quote: if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion

paragraphs.summary: The Board added two safeguards, including allowing reconsideration of Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence casts doubt on them.

propositions.text: On November 21, 2025, the Board issued a ruling with its conclusions on the preliminary issues, stating it was not a final determination on the Proposed Tariffs.
propositions.quote: the Board issued a ruling setting out its “conclusions on these preliminary issues” stating the ruling “does not constitute [the Board’s] final determinations on the Proposed Tariffs under consideration”

propositions.text: The Board reminded parties of the safeguard allowing reconsideration of Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence casts doubt.
propositions.quote: The Board also reminded the parties of its safeguard that “if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion”

paragraphs.summary: The Board issued a non-final ruling on preliminary issues and reminded parties of the safeguard for reconsideration based on Phase II evidence.

propositions.text: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.
propositions.quote: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN applied for judicial review of the Board's Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: The respondents move to strike SOCAN's application, arguing the Phase I Ruling is interlocutory and not a decision amenable to judicial review.
propositions.quote: They contend that the Phase I Ruling is an interlocutory one in a larger and ongoing administrative process and is therefore not a “decision” amenable to judicial review

propositions.text: Respondents argue that even if the ruling could be reviewed, SOCAN has not exhausted alternative recourse.
propositions.quote: that even if it were a decision that could be judicially reviewed in principle, SOCAN has not exhausted adequate and effective alternative recourse

propositions.text: Respondents argue no exceptional circumstances justify early judicial intervention.
propositions.quote: and that no exceptional circumstances exist to justify early judicial intervention.

propositions.text: Respondents seek $20,000 lump sum costs or heightened costs, arguing SOCAN’s application should never have been brought.
propositions.quote: These respondents seek lump sum costs of $20,000, or costs on a heightened basis, on the ground SOCAN’s application should never have been brought.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents move to strike, arguing the ruling is interlocutory, alternative recourse exists, no exceptional circumstances, and seek heightened costs from SOCAN.

propositions.text: SOCAN disagrees with respondents but argues that if the motion succeeds, heightened costs are not justified and $5,000 is appropriate.
propositions.quote: However, it contends that if the respondents’ motion is successful, heightened costs are not justified and that a $5,000 costs award is more appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN disagrees but argues that if it loses, only $5,000 in costs is appropriate, not heightened costs.

propositions.text: The motion to strike is granted and the application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Respondents are entitled to costs, but $5,000 is more appropriate than a heightened award.
propositions.quote: While I agree the respondents are entitled to costs, I agree with SOCAN that a costs award of $5,000 is more appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the motion to strike, dismisses SOCAN's application, and awards $5,000 in costs to respondents.

propositions.text: Respondents must show SOCAN’s application is so clearly improper as to be bereft of any possibility of success to succeed on this motion.
propositions.quote: the respondents must demonstrate that SOCAN’s application for judicial review is “so clearly improper as to be bereft of any possibility of success”

propositions.text: This is a high threshold to meet.
propositions.quote: This is admittedly a high threshold to meet.

paragraphs.summary: The court states respondents must show the application is clearly improper with no chance of success, a high threshold.

propositions.text: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike; facts in the notice of application are presumed true, with limited exceptions.
propositions.quote: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike, and with limited exceptions, we must presume the facts asserted in the notice of application are true

propositions.text: Documents referred to in the notice of application or incorporated by reference can be considered.
propositions.quote: documents referred to in the notice of application or incorporated by reference can be taken into account

propositions.text: Relevant documents here include the Phase I Notice, Phase I Ruling, and an earlier Board ruling CB-CDA 2025-004.
propositions.quote: Here, those documents include the Phase I Notice and the Phase I Ruling, as well as an earlier Board ruling, CB-CDA 2025-004 dated January 16, 2025.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the rules for motions to strike: presume facts in the notice, consider referenced documents, and lists relevant documents here.

propositions.text: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties must complete the administrative process before going to court.
propositions.quote: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties to an administrative process cannot proceed to the court system until that process has run its course

paragraphs.summary: The court states parties must finish the administrative process before seeking judicial review, unless exceptional circumstances exist.

propositions.text: This principle applies to all matters before the administrative decision maker.
propositions.quote: This principle applies “to all matters that arise” before the administrative decision maker

propositions.text: A procedural fairness concern does not meet the exceptional circumstances threshold.
propositions.quote: A procedural fairness concern does not meet the “exceptional circumstances” threshold

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies the rule applies to all matters before the administrative body and procedural fairness alone is not exceptional.

propositions.text: The rule prevents fragmentation, costs, delays, and waste from premature court proceedings and interlocutory judicial reviews.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this rule is to prevent “fragmentation of the administrative process and piecemeal court proceedings”, to eliminate “the large costs and delays associated with premature forays to court”, and to avoid “the waste associated with hearing an interlocutory judicial review when the applicant for judicial review may succeed at the end of the administrative process anyway”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the rule aims to prevent fragmented, costly, and wasteful premature court proceedings during ongoing administrative processes.

propositions.text: Bypassing the administrative process requires consequences of an interlocutory decision to be so immediate and radical as to call into question the rule of law.
propositions.quote: for an applicant to bypass the administrative process, “the consequences of an interlocutory decision [must] be so ‘immediate and radical’ that they call into question the rule of law”

paragraphs.summary: The court states only immediate and radical consequences justify bypassing the administrative process for judicial review.

propositions.text: SOCAN seeks to quash the Phase I Ruling and various declarations, including procedural fairness, errors, timing of decisions, and exceptions' applicability.
propositions.quote: SOCAN’s notice of application seeks an order quashing the Phase I Ruling as well as various declarations, including declarations that (i) the Board failed to discharge its duty of procedural fairness by deciding an issue that was outside the scope of Phase I; (ii) the Board erred in fact and law or reached a decision that is unreasonable; (iii) the Board shall not decide certain issues until the completion of Phase II; and (iv) two exceptions in the Copyright Act do not apply in particular circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN's application seeks to quash the Phase I Ruling and obtain declarations on fairness, errors, timing, and exceptions' applicability.

propositions.text: Despite the high threshold, the respondents have met it; SOCAN’s application is premature for stated reasons.
propositions.quote: the respondents have persuaded me that that threshold is met here. I find SOCAN’s application for judicial review premature for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondents have met the high threshold and SOCAN’s application is premature.

propositions.text: Only administrative action affecting rights, imposing obligations, or causing prejudicial effects is amenable to judicial review.
propositions.quote: only administrative action that affects rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects is amenable to judicial review

paragraphs.summary: The court states only administrative actions affecting rights, obligations, or causing prejudice can be judicially reviewed.

propositions.text: The Board’s final tariff decision after Phase II would be amenable to review, but the Phase I Ruling does not affect rights or obligations or cause prejudice warranting review now.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded the Phase I Ruling affects legal rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects to SOCAN that warrant judicial review at this stage of the proceeding.

propositions.text: The Phase I Ruling may affect the conduct of the proceeding, but that is true of many interlocutory orders.
propositions.quote: While I accept that the Phase I Ruling may affect the way the balance of the proceeding to determine the tariffs is conducted, that may be said of many interlocutory orders.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Phase I Ruling does not affect rights or obligations to warrant review, though it may affect the proceeding's conduct.

propositions.text: SOCAN argues the Board’s decision is final in substance regardless of its description.
propositions.quote: SOCAN posits that the Board’s decision is final in substance no matter how the Board describes it.

propositions.text: SOCAN says it is not alleging the Board intended to manipulate the prematurity doctrine.
propositions.quote: SOCAN says it is not suggesting that the Board intended to manipulate the prematurity doctrine.

propositions.text: SOCAN relies on Federal Court cases where administrative bodies tried to shield themselves from judicial review.
propositions.quote: Yet, it relies on Federal Court decisions where the relevant administrative decision maker was seen as trying to shield itself from judicial review

propositions.text: The circumstances here are not comparable to those in the cases SOCAN cites.
propositions.quote: The circumstances at issue here are simply not comparable to those addressed in those cases.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN argues the Board’s decision is final and cites cases, but the court finds those cases are not comparable to this situation.

propositions.text: SOCAN submits the Court has previously recognized a first Board order in a bifurcated proceeding as reviewable.
propositions.quote: SOCAN also submits that this Court has previously recognized a first order of the Board in a bifurcated proceeding as a matter amenable to judicial review.

propositions.text: The court agrees with respondents that CAIP is distinguishable from this case.
propositions.quote: But I agree with the respondents that Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Assn. of Internet Providers (C.A.), 2002 FCA 166 [CAIP] is distinguishable.

propositions.text: In CAIP, the Board’s first decision was final as it disentitled SOCAN from collecting royalties from an entire class of users.
propositions.quote: the decision under review in CAIP—the Board’s first decision in a bifurcated proceeding—disentitled SOCAN from collecting royalties from an entire class of users and thus was final in that respect

propositions.text: In CAIP, the parties consented to jurisdiction and prematurity was not addressed.
propositions.quote: the parties consented to the Court’s jurisdiction, and prematurity was not addressed

propositions.text: CAIP predates Democracy Watch, Toronto Port Authority, and Canadian Council for Refugees.
propositions.quote: Finally, CAIP predates Democracy Watch, Toronto Port Authority, and Canadian Council for Refugees.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN cites CAIP as precedent, but the court finds it distinguishable because it was final, consented, and predates relevant case law.

propositions.text: SOCAN’s reliance on Wilson is misplaced.
propositions.quote: SOCAN’s reliance on Wilson is misplaced.

propositions.text: In Wilson, the administrative decision maker bifurcated the proceeding into merits and remedy phases, creating a natural break.
propositions.quote: In Wilson the administrative decision maker bifurcated the proceeding into a merits and remedy phase—creating a “natural break between two separate phases of the proceedings”

propositions.text: Such bifurcation in Wilson often does not cause the ills identified in C.B. Powell.
propositions.quote: which, in the words of this Court, “often does not cause the ills identified in C.B. Powell”: Wilson at para. 36.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN's reliance on Wilson misplaced, explaining Wilson involved a different bifurcation that did not cause the same problems.

propositions.text: Here, the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties but has not yet applied the Phase I legal interpretations.
propositions.quote: here the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties but has yet to apply the legal interpretations set out in its Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: The impact of the Phase I Ruling will crystallize only when a formal tariff decision is made under the Copyright Act.
propositions.quote: the impact of the Phase I Ruling will crystallize only when a formal decision on the tariffs is made under the Copyright Act

propositions.text: Phase I and Phase II together concern the merits of the proceeding.
propositions.quote: Phase I and Phase II together concern the merits of the proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board's bifurcation differs from Wilson, as the Phase I Ruling's impact will only crystallize with the final tariff decision.

propositions.text: Even if the Phase I Ruling were reviewable, SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies.
propositions.quote: even if the Phase I Ruling were amenable to judicial review in principle, SOCAN has not exhausted the available alternative remedies.

propositions.text: The Phase I Ruling is preliminary and allows parties to ask the Board to reconsider if Phase II evidence casts doubt.
propositions.quote: The Phase I Ruling explicitly expresses its preliminary nature and acknowledges the parties’ right to ask the Board to reconsider a Phase I conclusion if the evidence in Phase II significantly throws that conclusion into doubt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies, as the Phase I Ruling is preliminary and reconsideration is possible after Phase II evidence.

propositions.text: SOCAN alleges the Board’s safeguard is inadequate and ineffective for two reasons.
propositions.quote: SOCAN alleges that the Board’s safeguard is inadequate and ineffective for two reasons.

propositions.text: Questions of law in the Phase I Ruling cannot be thrown into doubt by evidence.
propositions.quote: First, insofar as the Phase I Ruling addresses questions of law, they cannot be thrown into doubt by evidence.

propositions.text: The Board’s conclusions will limit the evidence that may be tendered in Phase II.
propositions.quote: Second, the Board’s conclusions will limit the evidence that may be tendered in Phase II.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN argues the Board's safeguard is inadequate because legal questions can't be revisited by evidence and Phase I limits Phase II evidence.

propositions.text: The Board is master of its own procedure.
propositions.quote: the Board is the master of its own procedure

propositions.text: The Board has broad discretion and powers over its processes, including witness examination and document production.
propositions.quote: the Board has broad discretion and powers concerning its processes, including the examination of witnesses and the production of documents

propositions.text: The Board can make case management orders, vary rules and orders, and grant leave to amend issues and records.
propositions.quote: the power to vary the rules governing its practice as appropriate, to vary orders made in a proceeding, and to grant leave to amend a statement of issues to be considered and a case record

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board has broad procedural powers, including case management, varying rules, and amending issues or records.

propositions.text: The Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of its case management powers.
propositions.quote: the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of its case management, as it was empowered to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board properly bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties under its case management authority.

propositions.text: Nothing precludes SOCAN from raising its judicial review issues before the Board in case management or during Phase II.
propositions.quote: I see nothing that precludes SOCAN from raising the matters it seeks to raise in its application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling before the Board, either in case management before Phase II starts (see paragraph 207 of the Phase I Ruling and paragraph 26 of the Phase I Notice), or during Phase II.

propositions.text: SOCAN has an alternative remedy it has not exhausted.
propositions.quote: SOCAN has an alternative remedy that it has not exhausted.

propositions.text: The Board has been transparent that Phase I conclusions may be revisited if Phase II evidence significantly throws them into doubt.
propositions.quote: the Board has been consistently transparent with the parties through the Phase I Notice and the Phase I Ruling—Phase I conclusions may be revisited should Phase II evidence significantly throw any one of them into doubt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN can raise its issues before the Board, which has been transparent about revisiting Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence warrants.

propositions.text: There are no exceptional circumstances justifying early court recourse regarding the Phase I Ruling.
propositions.quote: there are no exceptional circumstances that would justify early recourse to the courts in respect of the Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: The Phase I Ruling's consequences are not so immediate and radical as to call into question the rule of law.
propositions.quote: The consequences of the Phase I Ruling, as an interlocutory one, cannot be described in the terms outlined in Dugré and Wilson: the consequences are not so immediate and radical that they call into question the rule of law.

propositions.text: This situation is not analogous to circumstances justifying a writ of prohibition.
propositions.quote: the situation before me is not analogous to circumstances that could “justify the issuance of a writ of prohibition”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no exceptional circumstances exist to justify early judicial intervention regarding the Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: Even constitutional or jurisdictional questions do not attract interlocutory relief.
propositions.quote: “even constitutional questions or questions qualified as ‘jurisdictional’ questions cannot attract interlocutory relief”

propositions.text: The same applies here; the circumstances are not exceptional.
propositions.quote: The same must be said here—the circumstances are not exceptional.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that even constitutional or jurisdictional questions do not justify interlocutory relief, and the present circumstances are not exceptional.

propositions.text: At the end of Phase II, SOCAN may succeed in obtaining the tariffs it seeks.
propositions.quote: at the end of Phase II, SOCAN may succeed in obtaining the tariffs it seeks

propositions.text: If SOCAN does not succeed, it can challenge the decision by judicial review and is not precluded from raising current issues then.
propositions.quote: If it does not and chooses to challenge that decision by way of judicial review, SOCAN is not precluded from raising the matters raised in its current application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes SOCAN may still succeed after Phase II or raise its current issues in a later judicial review if needed.

propositions.text: SOCAN should raise issues before the Board, including alleged procedural fairness breaches.
propositions.quote: to the extent SOCAN can raise issues before the Board, including the alleged breach of procedural fairness, it is appropriate that it do so.

propositions.text: If SOCAN does not raise issues before the Board, it risks the Court not considering them on later judicial review.
propositions.quote: If it does not, but could have, it risks this Court exercising its discretion to not consider the issue on a subsequent application for judicial review

propositions.text: The Court will ordinarily not consider arguments on judicial review that were not made before the administrative decision-maker.
propositions.quote: This Court will ordinarily not consider on judicial review an argument that was not made before the administrative decision-maker.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN should raise issues before the Board or risk the Court declining to consider them in future judicial review.

propositions.text: The motion to strike is granted and the application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: If SOCAN seeks judicial review after Phase II, this dismissal is without prejudice to raising current issues, subject to stated principles.
propositions.quote: this dismissal is without prejudice to its right to then raise the issues it raises in its application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling, subject to the principles described in preceding paragraph.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the motion to strike, dismisses the application, and clarifies SOCAN can raise these issues after Phase II, subject to conditions.

propositions.text: Costs of $5,000 are awarded to the three respondents.
propositions.quote: I would award costs to the three respondents in the lump sum all-inclusive amount of $5,000.

paragraphs.summary: The court awards $5,000 in costs to the three respondents.
